newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Mathematicians mourn Hungary's "maths monk" Erdos.
newsitem.headline: Mathematicians mourn Hungary's "maths monk" Erdos.

text.p: Mathematicians from around the world said farewell on Friday to Hungary's wandering mathematical genius Paul Erdos, who died last month at the age of 83.

"This is the very last goodbye and it's very painful," said George Szekeres, a mathematician from Sydney, Australia, and lifelong friend of Erdos, who died in September while attending a conference in Warsaw.

"The entire world of mathematics will shed tears for him," Szekeres said, his voice cracking with emotion as he gave a short speech at a memorial service attended by some 500 people, many of them mathematicians, at a Budapest cemetery.

Erdos, who was Jewish and left Hungary in the 1930s when Jews were increasingly oppressed, was renowned in the maths world as a genius on the level of Albert Einstein, as a problem solver with no equal and for having no fixed abode.
His pioneering work in the field of combinatorics, a branch of mathematics that deals with arrangements of sets of points, is considered fundamental to the development of computers.
Yet Erdos lived what another speaker, mathematician Gyula Katona of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, called "the life of a monk of mathematics".
He had no house or flat, never married, had no children, carried little cash, had no credit cards and lived out of a suitcase containing a few changes of clothing and notebooks.
Erdos was renowned for calling colleagues from the airport to say "my brain is in town".
"He was a mathematicians' mathematician," John Selfridge, who was a graduate student at the University of California at Los Angeles when he met Erdos, told Reuters.
"He would pose a problem that a mathematician would be curious about and would say, "I think I agree with his conjecture. I think that's true...but the problem is to prove it'."
"Paul simply had to know and understand everything," said Ronald Graham, a vice-president of AT&T Laboratories-Research in the United States and past president of the American Mathematical Society.
Graham, who served for years as Erdos's financial manager, said he signed cheques for Erdos so often that eventually the bank was reluctant to accept Erdos's own signature.
"He lived with a little help from his friends and he had quite a few," Graham told Reuters.
"People would meet him at the airport. Quite often he would call to have someone meet him and you would show up to find out three or four other people had the same mission.
"One of the first things he did when he arrived at a place was to tell the people he had just left that he got there and to tell the people he's about to go and see ...of his progress."
Graham said mathematicians would need to study the 1,500 or so scholarly papers left behind by Erdos, whose cremated remains will be buried on Monday in a Jewish cemetery.
"He had a unique ability to identify problems which were just beyond what you could currently do," Graham said.
"It's easy to state impossible problems but he would state a problem whereby if you could solve this problem you would then know more than you knew before and open the door wider.
"It was like climbing a mountain and being able to drive one more piton in to be able to work your way up the mountain."
"He was without a doubt the most prodigious and prolific poser and he solved a lot of them...His death has left a void."
